meta.title: Who really said "Hope has two beautiful daughters; their names are Anger and Courage. Anger at the way things are, and Courage to see that they do not remain as they are"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not found in any work by Augustine. Wikiquote lists it as disputed; its earliest cited use is a 1988 Robert McAfee Brown book that gives no source.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hope has two beautiful daughters; their names are Anger and Courage. Anger at the way things are, and Courage to see that they do not remain as they are'?
meta.ogDescription: Widely credited to St. Augustine, but no one has found it in his works. It surfaces in late-1980s theology books that give no source.

answer.label: Not Augustine of Hippo — an unsourced modern attribution
answer.authorDates: Origin untraced · in print by the late 1980s
answer.sourceLine: No passage in Augustine’s works has been found that contains this line. Wikiquote files it under “Disputed,” and its only citation is a 1988 book by the theologian Robert McAfee Brown, which credits Augustine without naming a source. Brown later said he could not place it in Augustine’s writings either.

source.excerpt: Hope has two beautiful daughters. Their names are anger and courage; anger at the way things are, and courage to see that they do not remain the way they are.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line under “Disputed.” Its only citation is Robert McAfee Brown’s Spirituality and Liberation: Overcoming the Great Fallacy (1988), p. 136, which is a secondary source and not a work by Augustine.

The fact-check blog They Didn’t Say It ↗ (2018) found no Google Books results before 1987. It also reports that Brown himself, in Speaking of Christianity (p. 74), called it “a reflective comment whose location in the Augustinian corpus I wish I could pinpoint.”

A note under this entry on Wikiquote’s talk page ↗ reports that Brown’s acknowledgments (p. 11) thank Sr. Joan Delaplane, O.P., “for a quotation from Augustine … that has empowered me ever since I heard her use it.” That suggests he heard it spoken rather than read it in a text.
WIST Quotations ↗ marks the attribution “Spurious”: widely attributed to Augustine but not recognizably found in his works.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording Wikiquote transcribes from Brown’s 1988 book. The version that circulates online ends “as they are” rather than “the way they are.” Neither wording has been traced to Augustine.

source.rightsNote: This exact wording cannot be tied to any identifiable author or original work, so we assert no copyright status. Augustine’s genuine Latin writings are long in the public domain, but this line is not one of them. Brown’s 1988 book, where the line was printed and credited to someone else, is a modern copyrighted work.

author.name: Augustine of Hippo
author.heading: The man it’s credited to
author.bio: Aurelius Augustinus was a North African bishop and one of the most influential Church Fathers. His authentic works include the Confessions and The City of God. He wrote a great deal about hope, but this tidy “two daughters” line has not been found anywhere in his writings, and the person who actually coined it is unknown.

misattribution.heading: Why Augustine gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The line reads like a patristic aphorism, and Augustine wrote about hope at length. That has been enough for it to spread under his name through sermons, social-justice homilies and quote sites. No one who has checked has found it in his works.

items.why: The line is not found in his writings. Wikiquote ↗ files it as Disputed, and WIST ↗ calls it spurious, “not recognizably found in his works.”

Brown quoted it as Augustine’s in Spirituality and Liberation (1988), the citation Wikiquote ↗ gives. According to They Didn’t Say It ↗, he later admitted he could not pinpoint its location in Augustine. No one claims Brown wrote it himself.
As quoted by They Didn’t Say It ↗, Chaput wrote in Strangers in a Strange Land (p. 162): “The words are apocryphal. There’s no real evidence that Augustine ever wrote them.”

Maier built a March 2021 essay ↗ around the line but conceded the words “may not be his.” He wrote that an Augustine-scholar friend considers them apocryphal and that he has never been able to find their source.

misattribution.truthLine: The line has not been found in any work by Augustine. It appears in late-1980s theology writing that cites no source, and its real originator is unknown. See Wikiquote ↗ and They Didn’t Say It ↗.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The “two daughters” line became a favorite of social-justice and liberation-theology preaching because it treats anger as a companion of hope, not its enemy. Robert McAfee Brown, a Presbyterian theologian, put it in print in 1988 in Spirituality and Liberation, a book arguing that prayer and social action are two ways of talking about the same thing. From there it moved into homilies, parish bulletins and quote sites.

Even writers who love the line hedge it. In First Things ↗ (2021), Francis X. Maier wrote that the words are “attributed to St. Augustine” but “may not be his.” As reported by They Didn’t Say It ↗, Archbishop Chaput called them apocryphal while adding that their content is “clearly true and worth remembering.”
context.pull: “a reflective comment whose location in the Augustinian corpus I wish I could pinpoint” — Robert McAfee Brown, as quoted by They Didn’t Say It
